docs.text: A river's watershed is all the land that drains into it; rain falling anywhere inside the boundary eventually reaches the same channel.
Meandering rivers erode the outside of each bend and deposit sand on the inside, so the loops slowly migrate across the floodplain.
An oxbow lake forms when a meander is cut off from the main channel, leaving a curved pond beside the river.
Deltas grow where a river slows at the sea and drops its sediment faster than waves and tides can carry it away.
Levees are raised banks that keep floodwater in the channel, but they also stop silt from refreshing the surrounding fields.
Hydrologists measure discharge as the volume of water passing a point each second, usually in cubic meters per second.
Spring snowmelt can double a mountain stream's flow within days, then drop it back to a trickle by late summer.
Braided rivers split into many shallow channels that weave around gravel bars and shift after every flood.
Estuaries mix fresh river water with salty tidewater, creating nurseries for young fish and crabs.
Dams trap sediment behind them, so the river below often cuts deeper into its bed and starves beaches downstream of sand.
Earth reaches perihelion, its closest point to the Sun, in early January, about two weeks after the December solstice.
A light-year is a distance, not a time: roughly 9.46 trillion kilometers, the path light travels in one year.
Neutron stars pack more mass than the Sun into a sphere about twenty kilometers across.
The Moon always shows the same face to Earth because its rotation is tidally locked to its orbit.
Exoplanets are often found by the transit method: a star dims slightly and regularly as a planet passes in front of it.
Galaxies are moving apart because space itself is expanding, an observation first quantified by Edwin Hubble in 1929.
Meteor showers happen when Earth passes through a trail of dust left behind by a comet.
Saturn's rings are made mostly of ice chunks ranging from grains of dust to boulders the size of houses.
A total solar eclipse is visible only along a narrow path where the Moon's shadow touches the ground.
Red dwarf stars burn their fuel so slowly that they can shine for trillions of years.
Sous vide cooking seals food in a bag and holds it in a water bath at a precise temperature for a long time.
Searing meat browns its surface through the Maillard reaction, which creates hundreds of flavor compounds.
Bread rises because yeast eats sugars and releases carbon dioxide, which gluten traps in tiny bubbles.
Salting water for pasta seasons the noodles from the inside; it barely changes how fast the water boils.
A roux is flour cooked in fat, used to thicken sauces like béchamel and gumbo.
Resting a roast after cooking lets the juices redistribute so less runs out when you slice it.
Acid from lemon or vinegar brightens a heavy dish the way salt brings out sweetness.
Emulsions like mayonnaise hold oil and water together with the help of lecithin in egg yolk.
Caramelizing onions takes patience: low heat for forty minutes turns them sweet and deep brown.
Fermented foods such as kimchi and sauerkraut are preserved by lactic acid made by bacteria.
An octave doubles the frequency of a note, which is why the two sound like the same pitch at different heights.
A string quartet has two violins, a viola and a cello.
Syncopation places accents off the main beat, giving jazz and funk their forward push.
Equal temperament divides the octave into twelve identical semitones so every key sounds equally in tune.
The blues scale adds a flattened fifth, the so-called blue note, to the minor pentatonic scale.
A fugue introduces a short theme in one voice and then imitates it in others, layering them in counterpoint.
Tempo is measured in beats per minute; a slow ballad might sit around sixty, a dance track near one hundred twenty-eight.
Drummers keep time with the hi-hat while the kick and snare outline the groove.
Choirs sound full because many voices singing slightly different pitches blend into a rich chorus effect.
A guitar's frets are spaced closer together as they go up the neck because each semitone shortens the string by a fixed ratio.
Tachycardia means a resting heart rate above one hundred beats per minute in an adult.
Regular aerobic exercise lowers resting blood pressure and improves how the body handles blood sugar.
Adults generally need seven to nine hours of sleep; chronic short sleep is linked to poorer memory and mood.
Vaccines train the immune system by showing it a harmless piece or version of a pathogen.
Dehydration can cause headaches, dizziness and dark urine, especially after heavy sweating.
Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses such as the common cold.
A balanced plate is roughly half vegetables and fruit, a quarter whole grains and a quarter protein.
Washing hands with soap for twenty seconds removes many germs that spread respiratory infections.
Stretching after a workout can ease stiffness, though it does little to prevent next-day soreness.
Too much sun exposure without protection raises the long-term risk of skin cancer.
A hash table stores key-value pairs and finds items in roughly constant time by computing an index from the key.
Binary search finds an item in a sorted list by repeatedly halving the range, taking logarithmic time.
Garbage collection automatically frees memory that a program can no longer reach.
A compiler translates source code into machine instructions before the program runs.
Version control systems like Git record every change so a team can review history and undo mistakes.
Two-factor authentication asks for something you know and something you have, such as a code from your phone.
Caching keeps copies of recently used data in fast storage to avoid repeating slow work.
A race condition occurs when the result of a program depends on the unpredictable timing of threads.
Unit tests check small pieces of code in isolation so bugs are caught early.
Public-key cryptography lets anyone encrypt a message that only the holder of the private key can read.
In tennis, a score of forty-all is called deuce, and a player must then win two points in a row.
A marathon is 42.195 kilometers long, a distance fixed at the 1908 London Olympics.
In soccer, a player is offside if they are nearer the goal line than both the ball and the second-last defender when it is passed.
Swimmers shave seconds by streamlining underwater after each turn.
A cricket match can last five days in the test format, with breaks for lunch and tea.
Basketball's shot clock gives a team twenty-four seconds to attempt a shot in professional leagues.
Cyclists ride in a tight pack called a peloton to save energy by drafting behind each other.
A hat-trick is three goals scored by the same player in one game.
Rock climbers grade routes by difficulty, and bouldering problems are short, hard climbs without ropes.
Rowing crews synchronize their strokes because one late oar slows the whole boat.
Compound interest earns interest on previous interest, so savings grow faster the longer they are left alone.
Inflation reduces purchasing power: the same money buys fewer goods over time.
A diversified portfolio spreads money across many assets so one failure does less damage.
Index funds track a whole market rather than trying to pick winning stocks, which keeps fees low.
A credit score summarizes how reliably someone has repaid debts in the past.
Central banks raise interest rates to cool an overheating economy and cut them to encourage borrowing.
An emergency fund covering three to six months of expenses protects against job loss or sudden bills.
Bonds are loans to governments or companies that pay regular interest and return the principal at maturity.
A budget lists expected income and spending so you can see where money goes each month.
Paying only the minimum on a credit card lets high interest pile up for years.
Tomatoes need at least six hours of direct sun and consistent watering to avoid cracked fruit.
Composting turns kitchen scraps and leaves into dark, crumbly soil food over a few months.
Mulch keeps soil moist, suppresses weeds and moderates temperature around plant roots.
Pruning dead or crossing branches lets light and air into a shrub and reduces disease.
Legumes such as beans and peas host bacteria that fix nitrogen from the air into the soil.
Overwatering kills more houseplants than underwatering, because roots need air as well as water.
Bees and other pollinators are drawn to clusters of flowers in blue, purple and yellow.
Crop rotation moves plant families to new beds each year to break pest and disease cycles.
Seeds of many trees need a cold period over winter before they will sprout.
Raised beds warm up earlier in spring and drain better than flat ground.
Octopuses can change the color and texture of their skin in a fraction of a second to blend into their surroundings.
Coral reefs are built by tiny animals called polyps that secrete limestone skeletons.
Blue whales are the largest animals known to have lived, longer than a basketball court.
Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity pulling on Earth's oceans.
Deep-sea anglerfish lure prey with a glowing tip lit by symbiotic bacteria.
Sea turtles return to the beaches where they hatched to lay their own eggs.
Kelp forests grow in cool coastal water and can rise more than thirty meters toward the surface.
The ocean absorbs about a quarter of the carbon dioxide people emit, making seawater more acidic.
Dolphins identify each other with signature whistles, a little like names.
Hydrothermal vents on the seafloor support life that runs on chemical energy instead of sunlight.
The Roman aqueducts carried water for dozens of kilometers using only a gentle downhill slope.
The printing press, developed by Johannes Gutenberg around 1440, made books far cheaper to produce.
The Byzantine Empire continued the eastern Roman state for about a thousand years, with its capital at Constantinople.
Ancient Egyptians wrote on papyrus, a paper-like material made from reeds that grew along the Nile.
The Silk Road was a network of trade routes linking China with the Mediterranean world.
The Rosetta Stone carried the same decree in three scripts, which let scholars decipher hieroglyphs.
Medieval castles were built with thick walls and narrow windows to withstand sieges.
The Industrial Revolution began in Britain, where steam engines powered new factories.
The Great Wall of China was built and rebuilt over many centuries by different dynasties.
Vikings sailed shallow longships that could cross the open sea and still row far up rivers.
Hurricanes draw their energy from warm ocean water and weaken quickly over land.
A cold front can bring a sudden line of thunderstorms followed by cooler, drier air.
Fog is a cloud that forms at ground level when air cools to its dew point.
Lightning heats the air so fast that it expands explosively, which we hear as thunder.
Humidity makes hot days feel hotter because sweat evaporates more slowly.
Weather is the day-to-day state of the atmosphere, while climate is the long-term average.
Rainbows appear when sunlight is refracted and reflected inside raindrops, with the Sun behind you.
Tornadoes form from rotating thunderstorms called supercells.
Snowflakes grow as six-sided ice crystals, and their shape depends on temperature and humidity.
El Niño warms the eastern Pacific every few years and shifts rainfall patterns around the world.
High-speed trains use smooth, continuously welded rails and gentle curves to run safely above 300 kilometers per hour.
Electric cars convert most of their battery energy into motion, while petrol engines waste much of theirs as heat.
Container ships carry standardized steel boxes that move straight from ship to truck or train.
Airplanes fly because their wings push air downward, producing lift.
Bicycles are among the most energy-efficient ways to travel any distance.
Roundabouts reduce serious crashes because traffic moves slowly and in one direction.
Subway systems move huge numbers of people under crowded cities without using street space.
Pump model HX-4471 must be primed before its first start; running it dry voids the warranty.
Canals let barges carry heavy goods inland, using locks to climb and descend hills.
Jet lag happens when flying across time zones puts your body clock out of step with local daylight.
Morphemes are the smallest units of meaning; 'unhappiness' contains un-, happy and -ness.
Pidgins arise when speakers without a common language need to trade; creoles develop when children learn a pidgin as a first language.
English spelling is irregular partly because pronunciation changed after spelling was standardized by printers.
Tone languages such as Mandarin use pitch to distinguish words that otherwise sound the same.
Children acquire the grammar of their first language largely without explicit teaching.
Loanwords are words borrowed from other languages, like 'kindergarten' from German.
Sign languages are full natural languages with their own grammar, not codes for spoken words.
Zipf's law says a word's frequency is roughly inversely proportional to its rank in a frequency list.
Many languages put the verb last; Japanese and Turkish are well-known examples.
Dialects differ in vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation while remaining mutually understandable.
Dogs were domesticated from wolves tens of thousands of years ago and read human gestures remarkably well.
Cats spend much of the day asleep and are most active at dawn and dusk.
Migratory birds navigate using the Sun, the stars and Earth's magnetic field.
Honeybees perform a waggle dance to tell hive mates the direction and distance of flowers.
Elephants mourn their dead and can recognize the bones of relatives.
Crows solve multi-step puzzles and can even shape tools from twigs and wire.
Hibernating bears lower their metabolism for months and live off stored fat.
Frogs breathe partly through their skin, which makes them sensitive to pollution.
Cheetahs can sprint faster than one hundred kilometers per hour but only for short bursts.
A puppy's socialization window closes at around three to four months of age.
Flying buttresses let Gothic cathedrals have tall, thin walls filled with stained glass.
Reinforced concrete combines concrete's strength under compression with steel's strength under tension.
Passive houses use thick insulation and airtight construction to need very little heating.
Skyscrapers became practical with steel frames and safe passenger elevators.
The Roman Pantheon's dome is made of unreinforced concrete and has stood for nearly two thousand years.
Cantilevers project outward with support at only one end, like a balcony.
Green roofs covered in plants absorb rainwater and keep buildings cooler in summer.
Earthquake-resistant buildings use base isolators that let the ground move beneath them.
Arches carry weight by turning downward loads into sideways thrust along a curve.
Brutalist architecture favors raw concrete and bold, blocky forms.
